them which are taken for granted. But we must not forget
that there are situations in which a despised and outcast
person can shame us, so that he suddenly emerges as great
and we appear small in comparison. Jesus is fond of remind-
ing His hearers of situations like this. Just such a situation is
provided by the story of the Good Samaritan: the despised
and outcast Samaritan puts to shame the priest and Levite.
Most strange and scandalous! And here too: the despised
Publican towers high above the highly respected Pharisee
conscious of his rectitude. Most strange and scandalous!
Of course Jesus did not praise the Samaritan because he
was a Samaritan, but because he was merciful. Nor does He
here put the Publican above the Pharisee because he was a
Publican. He does not propose either to condemn the pious
zeal of the Pharisee, or to exonerate the vices incidental
to the calling of the Publican. But the vision of Jesus pierces
deeper than that superficial view of things with which we are
usually content. He sees that the true essential being of man
lies at a deeper level than that attitude which has become
normal for him as the member of a particular profession or
social class or even nation, whether good or bad. Yes, the
real being of a man lies on a deeper level. There are situations
in which it comes to light and those are the really decisive
situations. As in the story of the Good Samaritan the situation
is that a man sees someone lying wounded in a sinister
area and on a dangerous road, and it is then revealed whether
he realizes what is the meaning of love of one's neighbour,
so here the situation is that of prayer which discloses whether
one realizes what is man's true relation to God or not;
whether man is inwardly arrogant or humble, whether he—
as we may further say-knows himself or is self-deceived.
II
